Global Aviation Crisis

By: Sophia Phirippides | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
As lockdowns are extended all over the world, including South Africa, 2020 air flights are now expected to be half that of 2019 and the repercussions for the industry will be devastating.

Unique Selling Point:
The knock on effect of lockdown has well and truly begun and a snowball of economic deluge is on a roll. Not least in the aviation industry, with the exponential damage of that on the tourism industry. Worldwide travel restrictions to fight COVID-19 mean global aviation is on its knees. From South Africa to the rest of Africa, to the ends of the earth, it looks like all airlines will be in some form of business rescue pretty soon, predicts Guy Leitch editor of SA Flyer Magazine. So how devastating is this collapse and how are countries tackling the crisis of empty skies? And if air flights are already predicted to be half of that a year ago, what is the impact on jobs, GDP and how far does that impact spread and accumulate? Job losses and GDP decline, globally, will be dire indicators of the cost of strict travel restrictions and peoples’ recent reluctance to travel communally.

Summary:
With the massive drop in the number of passenger air flights, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) has updated its analysis of global airline passenger revenues concluding that they will plummet by 314 billion dollars this year, (55% compared to last year).
With such a drop in capital coming in not only small airlines will struggle to survive. Even the best positioned airlines have been put under liquidity pressure… with no money coming in, massive pressure has been put on their savings in hand. The savings of the large operators are depleting fast, which is why they are using vouchers for deferred travel so they can hold on to capital. It is also why governments have been put under severe pressure to fund airlines to keep them afloat. Most airlines have about a two month cash flow allowance with bigger airlines having slightly deeper pockets but as time marches on as does the corona virus, casualties are inevitable.
The scale of the decline can be seen in the struggles of the once apparently embedded players -like British Airways, who have announced they may have to shed 12000 jobs. Unlike some other European airlines whose governments are rescuing with money, British Airways is not being bailed out by the British government -some say in a tactical maneuver by BA to see off one of its main rivals Virgin Atlantic.
There is so much uncertainty in this new coronavirus era that the course of recovery is uncertain. To start with, no-one is clear as to when countries will actually lift travel restrictions as lockdown measures and timetables continue to be revised throughout the world. With such uncertainty people have begun to talk about a return to a “new normal” rather than a pre-COVID 19 normal, which the timescale to attain is now being talked about in terms of ‘years’.

Further information:
In Africa and particularly South Africa, airlines were already in a weak position on global comparisons before COVID-19 struck. We build our story from the local perspective, with the effect on domestic flights and broaden the narrative to the rest of Africa and the rest of the world. We have organised an interview with Wrenelle Stander, CEO of Comair. The once successful airline has been hit massively by lockdown, with no revenue coming in it is now desperately approaching its banks and government for financial assistance. Also scheduled is an interview with Tewolde GebreMariam, CEO of Ethiopian Airways, the star airways of Africa, as the story takes off internationally.

What of the cost to global tourism which the aviation industry used to fuel extensively? The United Nations World Tourism Organisation (UNWTO) forecast at the end of March that international tourism would decline by 20% to 30%, representing an estimated loss of 300 to 450 billion dollars in tourism receipts (a third of revenues in 2019).
Unlike the recovery from SARS, this will not be a quick bounce back, but industry watchers are now following China with interest. Their international flights are still curtailed but domestic flights are picking up - demand is now down 64% rather than down 80% from the month before. There is also hope for the aviation industry given by the fall in oil prices which may help to accelerate recovery even though the extent and speed of that recovery remains very uncertain, especially since there is no clarity about which airline operators will still be around to respond to an eventual increase in demand(aviation consultancy CAPA said earlier this month that by the end of May, "most airlines in the world will be bankrupt" without coordinated government and industry intervention).

China, the original epicentre, was the first to ban certain domestic and international travel to prevent the spread of the virus. The financial implications on the global industry were relatively limited, due to the monopoly of state-backed Chinese airlines in that market. With the virus’ spread to the other big aviation markets in Europe and then North America, the situation has really hit home for all.
The US restriction on European flights, for example, equates to around US$20bn in transatlantic passenger revenue annually. National air traffic navigation service providers covering the North Atlantic corridor are preparing for a drop in total traffic of approximately 85 percent. Internationally, travel bans as of late March could represent closer to 98 percent of global passenger revenue – with a three month blanket ban equivalent to over US$250bn.
Although President Trump signed a stimulus bill that includes $58 billion in aid for airlines — $29 billion in payroll grants for workers, and $29 billion in loans for the airlines — several US airlines have already collapsed. And it is likely that other airlines, both in the US and elsewhere, will be forced to consolidate or shut down, International Air Transport Association (IATA) director general Alexandre de Juniac has warned.
Here are the airlines that have collapsed, declared bankruptcy, or suspended operations so far:
UK regional airline Flybe entered administration — a practice similar to declaring bankruptcy — on Thursday, March 5. Although Flybe was already on the brink of collapse — despite a major investment by a Virgin Atlantic-led consortium the previous summer — the coronavirus crisis pushed it over the edge. Flybe operated about 40% of domestic flights in the UK.
Trans States Airlines is a Missouri-based regional airline that flies routes for United under the United Express brand. The airline had already been planning to shut down by the end of 2020, consolidating its operations with ExpressJet Airlines, another of United's regional carrier. However, due to the "unforeseen impact of the coronavirus," the airline will cease all operations on April 1, Trans States Holding CEO said in a memo to employees. Trans States operated a flight of Embraer ERJ-145 regional jets.
Compass Airlines - also owned by Trans States Holdings - also shut down in April. Compass is another regional carrier, which operates flights for American Airlines under its American Eagle brand. With American cutting domestic capacity by up to 80% by May, it's had less of a need for contract airlines.
Virgin Australia entered "voluntary administration," the Australian equivalent of Chapter 11 bankruptcy, on Tuesday, April 21. Although the Brisbane-based airline had suspended most of its operations and furloughed most of its employees, it was still losing money operating about 65 daily flights. The airline said it would continue operating during the restructuring process. It entered administration after a request for aid from the Australian government was denied.

Can the aviation industry bounce back?
Previous epidemics such as SARS also caused a sharp decline in air travel demand, but that followed a v-shaped drop with a quick bounce back. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) predicts the effects of COVID-19 to be much more far-reaching with a slower recovery, as there will inevitably be an economic recession in its wake. Personally, I think there will likely be the pent-up demand for a bounce back (once governments and the public feel they’ve contained things, of course). What is less clear is how rapidly the supply side can recover – with multiple operators realistically dropping out of the game, lessors having to work through major redeployment of assets, and those operators that continue with state bailouts needing years to regain their independence.

Interviews:
Guy Leitch speaks on the general crisis in aviation globally and talks about the knock on effect in industries - eg for every 24 dollars not spent on a ticket it's a 24 dollar loss to the tourism industry… etc
IATA - speak to the airline industry and what airlines are currently suffering under the strain. Which countries are assisting with bailouts and which airlines have deeper pockets
How the industry is trying to create a set of standards from check in right through to baggage control and inflight procedures to assure passengers that it would be safe to travel again.. Flying on the airplane itself is one of the safest and most controlled spaces in the value chain (with air conditioning up to the quality as used in operating theatres). They are trying to put together a set of protocols and safety measures that can be adopted worldwide so that the recovery does not suffer like the post 911 situation where there were totally different rules for different countries and different airlines. They talk on the very slow recovery of the industry for a number of factors… consumer confidence and uptake to travel, as well as how and when countries lift their travel bans.. The idea of quarantining passengers has been pushed aside as most people don't travel for longer than 10 days and that no-one willingly wants or can spend 14 days in quarantine before embarking on a journey so other protocols need to be put in place. The cost factor - what capacity the airlines would and can fly at to keep in line with safety and of course if the take-up on travel is slow only certain routes and flights can be opened by airlines which would again affect their bottom line.
Max Kingsley-Jones is the Exec Director Content for FlightGlobal Publishing in London. They produce the monthly Airline Business magazine, which is the equivalent of The Economist for the airline industry. He speaks to the plight of the smaller carriers throughout the world and how difficult some of them will find to sustain etc… He talks about BA and other airlines that are struggling to stay in the air, and what they will need to keep going. He is an independent voice and does not have any affiliations to any airlines. The US imposed different incentives to airlines which is why there are so many planes in the air. Basically in order to get the assistance of government there were to be no layoffs and the planes had to keep flying, even though there were no passengers, but that doesn't matter because they will be receiving government subsidy in order to do this.
Chris Zweigenthal CEO of the Airlines Association Southern Africa speaks to the plight of African Airlines, SAA and other local airlines that might find it difficult to keep going the longer the lockdown continues, but he is optimistic that solutions can be found to get air travel back up and running as soon as possible. He says that before Covid 19 African airlines were already struggling, and many battling to stay in the air, whereas internationally air travel had increased by 4% year on year, Africa's airlines were not experiencing growth, and now with COVID they are going to find it hardest to stay in the air. And especially in South Africa government doesn't have the kind of deep pockets that the US and some European countries have to bail out the airlines and to keep them going through the pandemic. There will be collateral damage along the way. Many airlines are retrenching some staff, paying them portions of their salaries in order to stay afloat. Coming out of COVID it will be a long time before jobs and the airlines will be restored to normality.
Chris comments on the co-dependency of the country’s airlines, airports, air navigation services, the SA Weather Service, the SA Civil Aviation Authority and others. The impact of the crisis does not just affect airlines, but the entire air transport system and every one of its constituent players.
He has some crucial things to say about the impact of the travel restrictions on the local air transport industry as there are some misconceptions and well-intended but poorly conceived regulations being proposed for the resumption of air services.

Press Release:


Locked international borders have grounded two thirds of the world’s passenger jets, losing airlines billions of dollars in revenue. Can the aviation industry survive the impact?

Script:


Annabel landing the plane… voice under…
Annabel: Oh, man, the day I got my wings in 2000 was the best day of my life because you work so hard for it and every single step was such an accomplishment and achievement.

VO: First Officer Annabel Vundla has been flying for over 20 years. She flew the presidential plane having trained in
the military.

Annabel: I was the only black woman to have qualified at that time, and it was extremely hard and difficult to have accomplished that.

VO: For the last 10 years she has flown as a commercial pilot for SAA, but the severe travel restrictions of the Coronavirus pandemic have changed everything.

Annabel: It's impacted every single pilot all over the world. You know, you just hope and pray that you still have a job.

LINK: The Covid-19 Pandemic has come at a great cost to world economies. But one of the biggest casualties is the Aviation Industry which has been decimated, with millions of passengers sitting at home and airlines grounded.


VO: Some of the world's leading aviation experts warn the impact is far-reaching.
VO: Alan Peaford: Chairman of the Aviation Africa Summit.

Alan: At the moment, it is facing the darkest time ever in its history. it is horrific with some of the biggest most successful airlines floundering and without government support we’d probably lose more than 80% of the world's airlines.


VO: Guy Leitch: Editor of SA Flyer in flight magazines.
Guy: There are increasing signs from the huge manufacturers of both Boeing and Airbus to say that they can't sustain it for the next 18 months as well without state assistance.

VO: Max Kingsley-Jones: Executive director of content for FlightGlobal.com.
Max: We've never seen and we've never modeled, I don’t think a kind of crisis that takes out the whole of the world's airlines effectively, simultaneously for a period of months.

Alexandre: For the past 50 years, probably since the Second World War. We haven't faced something so brutal, so deep, so negative.


VO: Alexandre de Juniac, CEO of The International Air Transport Association, IATA, which represents the bulk of the world's airlines, asserts that revenue loss for 2020 is estimated at over 320 billion dollars.

Alexandre: the number of jobs that depend directly or indirectly on airlines that could be impacted could reach the number of 25 million worldwide.


Link: The entire enterprise of flight is a feeder to many other industries and contributes to a broader economy worldwide.

VO: It is estimated that around two thirds of the world's passenger jets are grounded. Without significant government assistance, many prominent airlines will buckle under the strain, as their liquidity runs dry.
Max: Some of the bigger airlines are less financially secure than others. And some of the low cost carriers, like Ryanair or EasyJet, or in the States - Southwest, they've got very strong and deep pockets, but some of the national carriers certainly even in Europe, someone like Alitalia, they've already had to be effectively bailed out by the Italian government.

Mac: British Airways announced that it could be losing about 12,000 jobs.
Alan: If a company like British Airways is having to do that, then it shows how bad it is. Air Arabia, for example, have announced a redundancy package. Qatar Airways as well.

VO: In April the US government introduced a 50 billion dollar stimulus package incentivizing the country’s airlines to remain operational, even though aircraft have few passengers. Globally, IATA has liaised with almost 100 governments directly for assistance, including regulatory concessions.
Alexandre: To give you an example, some softening of the rules for passenger rights regarding the refund of unflown ticket. or to reduce taxes or to reduce overflight fees, to do everything they can to reduce our cost.

VO: This reduction in costs will help to uplift the airline industry and at the forefront of its value chain is tourism which is in critical condition. Africa’s travel and tourism sector alone contributes 169 billion dollars to the continent’s economy.

Alan: It's not just the cost of an air ticket. We're talking about the hotels and restaurants and taxi drivers and souvenir shops and just about everything else that ties around bringing tourists in.


VO: Chris Zweigenthal, CEO of the Airlines Association of Southern Africa cautions there will be grave consequences if air travel restrictions are extended beyond 3 months.

Chris: In South Africa, the airline industry was supporting 472,000 jobs if you extend that into travel and tourism. The latest estimate from IATA is that 252,000 jobs of that 472,000 are at risk. So it's really a dire situation.

VO: But there are carriers on the continent like Ethiopian Airlines that are proving to be resilient. Chief Commercial Officer Esayas Hailu, attributes this to their diversified business model which encompasses aviation services and the hotel and hospitality industry.

Esayas: We have a large cargo network. Now we are even converting passenger aircrafts into cargo aircrafts by removing chairs and loading above and below the wing.

VO: Esayas Hailu is convinced there are opportunities for other African carriers in the cargo market.

Esayas: I’m advising our colleagues, they can use passenger aircraft to uplift perishables at least it can cover the operating costs.

Alan: We've seen massive amounts of fresh produce rotting in Nairobi because there are no passenger aeroplanes with the hold available to take the fresh fruit that's coming to Europe. In South Africa and in Kenya as well, any of the International carriers will carry fresh flowers back to their markets.That's gone.

VO: South African aviation had already experienced turbulence before the pandemic with two of its state owned airlines SAA and SA Express in business rescue.
And, with the State of Disaster forcing Comair’s fleet to ground, the cash-strapped private company has now entered voluntary business rescue. But they remain solvent and are hopeful that operations will resume in November.

Chris: We have eight commercial scheduled Airlines flying in South Africa, three of them are state owned airlines and five of them are private airlines. And all of them are going through difficulties in terms of cash availability, and all of them are taking measures to preserve their cash.


VO: Pre-covid-19, airlines in South Africa had on average, a two month liquidity window. Now time is running out.

Nico: I am not aware of an airline that can turn around and say that they're not nervous, that they're not impacted by this event. And that includes Mango.


VO: CEO of Mango Airlines Nico Bezuidenhout, is managing to keep the 13 year old State owned carrier above water.

Nico: Mango's definitely got one of the most cost efficient cost structures in the country So aircraft leases for example, you're due to pay aircraft leases, but the aircraft is not flying. We have negotiated with our aircraft lessors. We have received concessions from our employee pool because those two elements are typically your biggest single fixed cost elements.


VO: Globally the industry needs to get back in the air, but analysts predict that it could take between 18 months and three years to see it recover to 2019 figures.

Guy: I think we're going to have seen a lot of consolidation amongst the weaker airlines. And so there'll be less competition, which will drive prices up. probably to as much as 50%. But the expectation is that next year, ticket prices will become cheaper while the airlines seek to fill the seats.


Link: One of the biggest barriers for the aviation industry on its path to recovery, will be people’s reluctance to travel in groups once lockdown restrictions are eased worldwide. So how will airlines get passengers to feel safe to fly again?

Alexandre: We could go from temperature check to wear a mandatory mask on board, plus a health declaration potentially, some precautions on board, to simplify the embarkment and to avoid people being too close.


VO: IATA together with industry stakeholders are formulating protocols for the entirety of a passenger’s journey, including whether, neutralizing the middle seat on wide bodied aircraft, is necessary.

Alexandre: We think that if you have a mask, if you have been checked for your temperature, if the aircraft has been sanitised, it's not necessary to neutralise the middle seat.


VO: Until treatments or a vaccine for COVID-19 are made available, the picture of aviation in the foreseeable future will be tentative with a phased restart.

Guy: I think that the entire airline industry will ultimately come to be changed by the move towards video conferencing, webinars, etc, and I think that'll take a large portion of the premium travel market out of the airline industry

Alexandre: The worrisome element is that we forecast that the traffic by the end of 2020 should be between 50 to 60% of the 2019 reference.


VO: But for now aircraft by the thousands are parked scattered around the world with many of their employees eager to soar again.

Annabel: it's heart wrenching that we can't carry out our passion and sit in our offices at 35,000 feet and look at the beautiful clouds

Internationally, travel bans as of late March could represent closer to 98 percent of global passenger revenue – with a three month blanket ban equivalent to over US$250bn. Although President Trump signed a stimulus bill that includes $58 billion in aid for airlines — $29 billion in payroll grants for workers, and $29 billion in loans for the airlines — several US airlines have already collapsed. And it is likely that other airlines, both in the US and elsewhere, will be forced to consolidate or shut down, International Air Transport Association (IATA) director general Alexandre de Juniac has warned. Here are the airlines that have collapsed, declared bankruptcy, or suspended operations so far: UK regional airline Flybe entered administration — a practice similar to declaring bankruptcy — on Thursday, March 5. Although Flybe was already on the brink of collapse — despite a major investment by a Virgin Atlantic-led consortium the previous summer — the coronavirus crisis pushed it over the edge. Flybe operated about 40% of domestic flights in the UK. Trans States Airlines is a Missouri-based regional airline that flies routes for United under the United Express brand. The airline had already been planning to shut down by the end of 2020, consolidating its operations with ExpressJet Airlines, another of United's regional carrier. However, due to the "unforeseen impact of the coronavirus," the airline will cease all operations on April 1, Trans States Holding CEO said in a memo to employees. Trans States operated a flight of Embraer ERJ-145 regional jets. Compass Airlines - also owned by Trans States Holdings - also shut down in April. Compass is another regional carrier, which operates flights for American Airlines under its American Eagle brand. With American cutting domestic capacity by up to 80% by May, it's had less of a need for contract airlines. Virgin Australia entered "voluntary administration," the Australian equivalent of Chapter 11 bankruptcy, on Tuesday, April 21. Although the Brisbane-based airline had suspended most of its operations and furloughed most of its employees, it was still losing money operating about 65 daily flights. The airline said it would continue operating during the restructuring process. It entered administration after a request for aid from the Australian government was denied. Can the aviation industry bounce back? Previous epidemics such as SARS also caused a sharp decline in air travel demand, but that followed a v-shaped drop with a quick bounce back. The International Air Transport Association (IATA) predicts the effects of COVID-19 to be much more far-reaching with a slower recovery, as there will inevitably be an economic recession in its wake. Personally, I think there will likely be the pent-up demand for a bounce back (once governments and the public feel they’ve contained things, of course). What is less clear is how rapidly the supply side can recover – with multiple operators realistically dropping out of the game, lessors having to work through major redeployment of assets, and those operators that continue with state bailouts needing years to regain their independence. They are trying to put together a set of protocols and safety measures that can be adopted worldwide so that the recovery does not suffer like the post 911 situation where there were totally different rules for different countries and different airlines. They talk on the very slow recovery of the industry for a number of factors… consumer confidence and uptake to travel, as well as how and when countries lift their travel bans.. The idea of quarantining passengers has been pushed aside as most people don't travel for longer than 10 days and that no-one willingly wants or can spend 14 days in quarantine before embarking on a journey so other protocols need to be put in place. The cost factor - what capacity the airlines would and can fly at to keep in line with safety and of course if the take-up on travel is slow only certain routes and flights can be opened by airlines which would again affect their bottom line. Max Kingsley-Jones is the Exec Director Content for FlightGlobal Publishing in London. They produce the monthly Airline Business magazine, which is the equivalent of The Economist for the airline industry. He speaks to the plight of the smaller carriers throughout the world and how difficult some of them will find to sustain etc… He talks about BA and other airlines that are struggling to stay in the air, and what they will need to keep going. He is an independent voice and does not have any affiliations to any airlines. The US imposed different incentives to airlines which is why there are so many planes in the air. Basically in order to get the assistance of government there were to be no layoffs and the planes had to keep flying, even though there were no passengers, but that doesn't matter because they will be receiving government subsidy in order to do this. Chris Zweigenthal CEO of the Airlines Association Southern Africa speaks to the plight of African Airlines, SAA and other local airlines that might find it difficult to keep going the longer the lockdown continues, but he is optimistic that solutions can be found to get air travel back up and running as soon as possible. He says that before Covid 19 African airlines were already struggling, and many battling to stay in the air, whereas internationally air travel had increased by 4% year on year, Africa's airlines were not experiencing growth, and now with COVID they are going to find it hardest to stay in the air. And especially in South Africa government doesn't have the kind of deep pockets that the US and some European countries have to bail out the airlines and to keep them going through the pandemic. There will be collateral damage along the way. Many airlines are retrenching some staff, paying them portions of their salaries in order to stay afloat. Coming out of COVID it will be a long time before jobs and the airlines will be restored to normality. Chris comments on the co-dependency of the country’s airlines, airports, air navigation services, the SA Weather Service, the SA Civil Aviation Authority and others. The impact of the crisis does not just affect airlines, but the entire air transport system and every one of its constituent players. He has some crucial things to say about the impact of the travel restrictions on the local air transport industry as there are some misconceptions and well-intended but poorly conceived regulations being proposed for the resumption of air services. LATHAM LAA016 TX Details Back references from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 24 May 2020 - Carte Blanche HD mihle@combinedartists.co.za 11 June 2020 Press Release: Locked international borders have grounded two thirds of the world’s passenger jets, losing airlines billions of dollars in revenue. Can the aviation industry survive the impact? Script: Annabel landing the plane… voice under… Annabel: Oh, man, the day I got my wings in 2000 was the best day of my life because you work so hard for it and every single step was such an accomplishment and achievement. VO: First Officer Annabel Vundla has been flying for over 20 years. She flew the presidential plane having trained in the military. Annabel: I was the only black woman to have qualified at that time, and it was extremely hard and difficult to have accomplished that. VO: For the last 10 years she has flown as a commercial pilot for SAA, but the severe travel restrictions of the Coronavirus pandemic have changed everything. Annabel: It's impacted every single pilot all over the world. You know, you just hope and pray that you still have a job. LINK: The Covid-19 Pandemic has come at a great cost to world economies. But one of the biggest casualties is the Aviation Industry which has been decimated, with millions of passengers sitting at home and airlines grounded. VO: Some of the world's leading aviation experts warn the impact is far-reaching. VO: Alan Peaford: Chairman of the Aviation Africa Summit. Alan: At the moment, it is facing the darkest time ever in its history. it is horrific with some of the biggest most successful airlines floundering and without government support we’d probably lose more than 80% of the world's airlines. VO: Guy Leitch: Editor of SA Flyer in flight magazines. Guy: There are increasing signs from the huge manufacturers of both Boeing and Airbus to say that they can't sustain it for the next 18 months as well without state assistance. VO: Max Kingsley-Jones: Executive director of content for FlightGlobal.com. Max: We've never seen and we've never modeled, I don’t think a kind of crisis that takes out the whole of the world's airlines effectively, simultaneously for a period of months. Alexandre: For the past 50 years, probably since the Second World War. We haven't faced something so brutal, so deep, so negative. VO: Alexandre de Juniac, CEO of The International Air Transport Association, IATA, which represents the bulk of the world's airlines, asserts that revenue loss for 2020 is estimated at over 320 billion dollars. Alexandre: the number of jobs that depend directly or indirectly on airlines that could be impacted could reach the number of 25 million worldwide. Link: The entire enterprise of flight is a feeder to many other industries and contributes to a broader economy worldwide. VO: It is estimated that around two thirds of the world's passenger jets are grounded. Without significant government assistance, many prominent airlines will buckle under the strain, as their liquidity runs dry. Max: Some of the bigger airlines are less financially secure than others. And some of the low cost carriers, like Ryanair or EasyJet, or in the States - Southwest, they've got very strong and deep pockets, but some of the national carriers certainly even in Europe, someone like Alitalia, they've already had to be effectively bailed out by the Italian government. Mac: British Airways announced that it could be losing about 12,000 jobs. Alan: If a company like British Airways is having to do that, then it shows how bad it is. Air Arabia, for example, have announced a redundancy package. Qatar Airways as well. VO: In April the US government introduced a 50 billion dollar stimulus package incentivizing the country’s airlines to remain operational, even though aircraft have few passengers. Globally, IATA has liaised with almost 100 governments directly for assistance, including regulatory concessions. Alexandre: To give you an example, some softening of the rules for passenger rights regarding the refund of unflown ticket. or to reduce taxes or to reduce overflight fees, to do everything they can to reduce our cost. VO: This reduction in costs will help to uplift the airline industry and at the forefront of its value chain is tourism which is in critical condition. Africa’s travel and tourism sector alone contributes 169 billion dollars to the continent’s economy. Alan: It's not just the cost of an air ticket. We're talking about the hotels and restaurants and taxi drivers and souvenir shops and just about everything else that ties around bringing tourists in. VO: Chris Zweigenthal, CEO of the Airlines Association of Southern Africa cautions there will be grave consequences if air travel restrictions are extended beyond 3 months. Chris: In South Africa, the airline industry was supporting 472,000 jobs if you extend that into travel and tourism. The latest estimate from IATA is that 252,000 jobs of that 472,000 are at risk. So it's really a dire situation. VO: But there are carriers on the continent like Ethiopian Airlines that are proving to be resilient. Chief Commercial Officer Esayas Hailu, attributes this to their diversified business model which encompasses aviation services and the hotel and hospitality industry. Esayas: We have a large cargo network. Now we are even converting passenger aircrafts into cargo aircrafts by removing chairs and loading above and below the wing. VO: Esayas Hailu is convinced there are opportunities for other African carriers in the cargo market. Esayas: I’m advising our colleagues, they can use passenger aircraft to uplift perishables at least it can cover the operating costs. Alan: We've seen massive amounts of fresh produce rotting in Nairobi because there are no passenger aeroplanes with the hold available to take the fresh fruit that's coming to Europe. In South Africa and in Kenya as well, any of the International carriers will carry fresh flowers back to their markets.That's gone. VO: South African aviation had already experienced turbulence before the pandemic with two of its state owned airlines SAA and SA Express in business rescue. And, with the State of Disaster forcing Comair’s fleet to ground, the cash-strapped private company has now entered voluntary business rescue. But they remain solvent and are hopeful that operations will resume in November. Chris: We have eight commercial scheduled Airlines flying in South Africa, three of them are state owned airlines and five of them are private airlines. And all of them are going through difficulties in terms of cash availability, and all of them are taking measures to preserve their cash. VO: Pre-covid-19, airlines in South Africa had on average, a two month liquidity window. Now time is running out. Nico: I am not aware of an airline that can turn around and say that they're not nervous, that they're not impacted by this event. And that includes Mango. VO: CEO of Mango Airlines Nico Bezuidenhout, is managing to keep the 13 year old State owned carrier above water. Nico: Mango's definitely got one of the most cost efficient cost structures in the country So aircraft leases for example, you're due to pay aircraft leases, but the aircraft is not flying. We have negotiated with our aircraft lessors. We have received concessions from our employee pool because those two elements are typically your biggest single fixed cost elements. VO: Globally the industry needs to get back in the air, but analysts predict that it could take between 18 months and three years to see it recover to 2019 figures. Guy: I think we're going to have seen a lot of consolidation amongst the weaker airlines. And so there'll be less competition, which will drive prices up. probably to as much as 50%. But the expectation is that next year, ticket prices will become cheaper while the airlines seek to fill the seats. Link: One of the biggest barriers for the aviation industry on its path to recovery, will be people’s reluctance to travel in groups once lockdown restrictions are eased worldwide. So how will airlines get passengers to feel safe to fly again? Alexandre: We could go from temperature check to wear a mandatory mask on board, plus a health declaration potentially, some precautions on board, to simplify the embarkment and to avoid people being too close. VO: IATA together with industry stakeholders are formulating protocols for the entirety of a passenger’s journey, including whether, neutralizing the middle seat on wide bodied aircraft, is necessary. Alexandre: We think that if you have a mask, if you have been checked for your temperature, if the aircraft has been sanitised, it's not necessary to neutralise the middle seat. VO: Until treatments or a vaccine for COVID-19 are made available, the picture of aviation in the foreseeable future will be tentative with a phased restart. Guy: I think that the entire airline industry will ultimately come to be changed by the move towards video conferencing, webinars, etc, and I think that'll take a large portion of the premium travel market out of the airline industry Alexandre: The worrisome element is that we forecast that the traffic by the end of 2020 should be between 50 to 60% of the 2019 reference. VO: But for now aircraft by the thousands are parked scattered around the world with many of their employees eager to soar again. Annabel: it's heart wrenching that we can't carry out our passion and sit in our offices at 35,000 feet and look at the beautiful clouds

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): As lockdowns are extended all over the world, including South Africa, 2020 air flights are now expected to be half that of 2019 and the repercussions for the industry will be devastating.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The knock on effect of lockdown has well and truly begun and a snowball of economic deluge is on a roll. Not least in the aviation industry, with the exponential damage of that on the tourism industry. Worldwide travel restrictions to fight COVID-19 mean global aviation is on its knees. From South Africa to the rest of Africa, to the ends of the earth, it looks like all airlines will be in some form of business rescue pretty soon, predicts Guy Leitch editor of SA Flyer Magazine. So how devastating is this collapse and how are countries tackling the crisis of empty skies? And if air flights are already predicted to be half of that a year ago, what is the impact on jobs, GDP and how far does that impact spread and accumulate? Job losses and GDP decline, globally, will be dire indicators of the cost of strict travel restrictions and peoples’ recent reluctance to travel communally.
metadata.Summary: With the massive drop in the number of passenger air flights, the International Air Transport Association (IATA) has updated its analysis of global airline passenger revenues concluding that they will plummet by 314 billion dollars this year, (55% compared to last year). With such a drop in capital coming in not only small airlines will struggle to survive. Even the best positioned airlines have been put under liquidity pressure… with no money coming in, massive pressure has been put on their savings in hand. The savings of the large operators are depleting fast, which is why they are using vouchers for deferred travel so they can hold on to capital. It is also why governments have been put under severe pressure to fund airlines to keep them afloat. Most airlines have about a two month cash flow allowance with bigger airlines having slightly deeper pockets but as time marches on as does the corona virus, casualties are inevitable. The scale of the decline can be seen in the struggles of the once apparently embedded players -like British Airways, who have announced they may have to shed 12000 jobs. Unlike some other European airlines whose governments are rescuing with money, British Airways is not being bailed out by the British government -some say in a tactical maneuver by BA to see off one of its main rivals Virgin Atlantic. There is so much uncertainty in this new coronavirus era that the course of recovery is uncertain. To start with, no-one is clear as to when countries will actually lift travel restrictions as lockdown measures and timetables continue to be revised throughout the world. With such uncertainty people have begun to talk about a return to a “new normal” rather than a pre-COVID 19 normal, which the timescale to attain is now being talked about in terms of ‘years’.
